name: Yosemite National Park
tagline: Big granite views from paved paths. Almost no trails.
summary: Yosemite follows the standard national park rule: dogs stay on pavement and in campgrounds. That still gets you Yosemite Falls, El Capitan Meadow, Glacier Point and a lot of riverbank. What it does not get you is any real hiking, and no lodge or tent cabin in the park takes pets.
verdict: Bring your dog for a camping trip with easy valley strolls. Leave them home if hiking is the point of the trip.

photo.alt: El Capitan rising above a grassy meadow and tall pine trees in Yosemite Valley
photo.author: Adam Kool

glance.note: Paved paths and one meadow loop only
Most drive-in campgrounds; not Camp 4 or group sites
No pets in any lodge, cabin or tent cabin inside the park
Merced River banks next to paved paths and campgrounds
6 ft or shorter, at all times
No pet fee. $35 per car entry, good for 7 days

allowed.name: Paved roads, sidewalks and bike paths
allowed.detail: This is the big one. Yosemite Valley has about 12 miles of paved multi-use path, and dogs are welcome on all of it unless a sign says otherwise.

allowed.name: Lower Yosemite Fall loop
allowed.detail: A flat, paved 1-mile loop to the base of the falls. The best short walk in the park with a dog, and loudest in May and June.

allowed.name: Bridalveil Fall path
allowed.detail: Short paved walk from the parking area to the viewing spot at the bottom of the fall. Expect spray in spring.

allowed.name: Glacier Point
allowed.detail: The paved 0.3-mile path from the parking lot to the famous overlook is open to dogs. Road usually open late May to October.

allowed.name: Wawona Meadow Loop
allowed.detail: The one real trail dogs may use: a 3.5-mile dirt loop road around Wawona Meadow, near the Wawona Hotel.

allowed.name: Campgrounds
allowed.detail: Every drive-in campground, except walk-in campgrounds like Camp 4 and all group sites.

allowed.name: Picnic areas and parking lots
allowed.detail: Including Cathedral Beach, Swinging Bridge, El Capitan and Church Bowl picnic areas.

notAllowed.name: Every unpaved trail
notAllowed.detail: That includes the Mist Trail, Four Mile Trail, Mirror Lake trail, Vernal Fall and Nevada Fall. The paved road to Mirror Lake is fine; the dirt loop around it is not.

notAllowed.name: Mariposa Grove of Giant Sequoias
notAllowed.detail: No dogs anywhere in the grove, carried or not. Try the paved path at Tuolumne Grove instead, and stay on the pavement there.

notAllowed.name: Shuttle buses
notAllowed.detail: Dogs cannot ride the free Valley or Mariposa Grove shuttles, so plan to park near what you want to see.

notAllowed.name: Lodging and tent cabins
notAllowed.detail: The Ahwahnee, Yosemite Valley Lodge, Curry Village, Housekeeping Camp, Wawona Hotel and White Wolf do not take pets.

notAllowed.name: Buildings
notAllowed.detail: Visitor centers, stores and restaurants. Patios are at the manager's discretion.

notAllowed.name: Wilderness and backcountry
notAllowed.detail: No dogs on any backpacking route or in the High Sierra Camps.

hikes.name: Lower Yosemite Fall Loop
hikes.why: Flat, shaded and ends at the base of a 320-foot waterfall. Benches along the way for rests.

hikes.name: Yosemite Valley Loop (bike path)
hikes.distance: Up to 12 mi, pick any section
hikes.why: Walk as little or as much as you like under El Capitan and Half Dome. The Cook's Meadow and Sentinel Bridge section is the most scenic mile.

hikes.name: Wawona Meadow Loop
hikes.why: The only unpaved route open to dogs. Flat, quiet, wildflowers in June and far fewer people than the Valley.

hikes.name: Bridalveil Fall
hikes.why: Ten minutes to a 620-foot waterfall. Good first stop coming in from the south entrance.

hikes.name: Glacier Point Overlook
hikes.why: The best view in the park for the least effort. Half Dome straight ahead, the Valley 3,200 feet below.

hangouts.name: Cook's Meadow and Sentinel Bridge
hangouts.why: Classic Half Dome reflection spot at sunset, right off the paved path.

hangouts.name: Cathedral Beach picnic area
hangouts.why: Sandy river bar on the Merced with El Capitan straight across. Dogs on leash can wade at the edge.

hangouts.name: El Capitan Meadow
hangouts.why: Lie back and watch climbers on the wall. Stay on the roadside edge, as the meadow interior is closed for restoration.

hangouts.name: Tunnel View
hangouts.why: The postcard view, from a paved parking lot. No walking required.

hangouts.name: Tuolumne Meadows (summer)
hangouts.why: Paved road shoulders and the campground at 8,600 feet, cool when the Valley is hot. Tioga Road opens around late May.

rules: Keep your dog on a leash no longer than 6 feet, at all times, everywhere.
Stay on pavement, in campgrounds or in picnic areas. Carrying a dog does not make a trail legal.
Never leave a dog unattended, including tied up at a campsite or in a parked car.
Pick up waste and put it in a trash can, not a bear box.
Store dog food in the bear locker at your campsite, never in your car or tent.
Dogs cannot ride any park shuttle bus.
Rangers can fine you for violations. Fines start at $100 and go up for repeat offences.
Service dogs are allowed everywhere; emotional support animals follow the pet rules.

camping.name: Upper Pines, Lower Pines and North Pines
camping.note: In Yosemite Valley. Reserve on Recreation.gov up to 5 months ahead; they sell out in minutes.

camping.name: Wawona Campground
camping.note: South end of the park, next to the Wawona Meadow Loop. Best base for dog owners.

camping.name: Hodgdon Meadow Campground
camping.note: Near the Big Oak Flat entrance, open year-round. Pets in standard sites only.

camping.name: Bridalveil Creek and Tuolumne Meadows
camping.note: Summer-only high country campgrounds. Pets OK in standard sites, not group sites.

lodging.name: Tenaya at Yosemite, Fish Camp
lodging.note: 2 miles from the south entrance. Pet rooms with a fee, dog beds and a welcome kit.

lodging.name: Yosemite View Lodge, El Portal
lodging.note: On the Merced River at the Arch Rock entrance. Pet-friendly rooms.

lodging.name: Vacation rentals in Yosemite West and Wawona
lodging.note: Inside the park boundary; many allow dogs. Check the listing.

lodging.name: Rush Creek Lodge and Evergreen Lodge, Groveland
lodging.note: Pet-friendly rooms near the Big Oak Flat entrance.

boarding.name: Tenaya at Yosemite kennel and dog-sitting
boarding.note: Day kennel and sitters for guests, advance notice required. Lets you hike the Mist Trail or Mariposa Grove.

boarding.name: Yosemite Valley Stable kennel
boarding.note: Reports conflict on whether the seasonal in-park kennel still runs. Call the park at (209) 372-0200 before relying on it.

seasons.title: Spring (April to June)
seasons.detail: Waterfalls at full roar and the paved paths are at their best. Expect spray at Lower Yosemite Fall and Bridalveil.

seasons.title: Summer heat and crowds
seasons.detail: Valley pavement reaches paw-burning temperatures by midday in July and August. Walk early, and bring more water than you think.

seasons.title: Reservations
seasons.detail: Peak-season entry reservations have been required in recent summers. Check the park website before you drive up.

seasons.title: Winter
seasons.detail: Glacier Point Road and Tioga Road close with snow. The Valley stays open and quiet, and dogs are fine on plowed paths.

wildlife: Black bears live throughout the park. Keep dog food, bowls and treats in the bear locker.
Coyotes hunt in the Valley meadows and will approach small dogs. Keep the leash short at dawn and dusk.
Rattlesnakes are common below 7,000 feet on sunny rock and roadsides from spring to fall.
Foxtails (barbed grass seeds) fill the meadows in summer and can lodge in paws, ears and noses.
checklist: Water for two, and a collapsible bowl
A 6-foot leash, not a retractable one
Waste bags and a way to carry them back to a bin
Paw balm or booties for hot pavement
Current vaccination records if you plan to use a kennel
A photo of your dog and an ID tag with your mobile number
A cooling mat for the campsite in summer
